themes.name: Things That Bend Your Brain
themes.tagline: Physics and math that rewards the second look — where the popular explanation turns out to be the wrong one.

items.title: Electricity and Magnetism AREN'T the Same: Relativity & The Meaning of Lorentz Invariance
items.description: Are Magnetism and Electricity the same thing? This idea, propounded by numerous YouTubers, physicists, and even many textbooks, relies on a rather fanciful mathematical trick involving the Lorentz transformations and the set-up of a current driven through a thin wire. But do the mathematics really hold up to scrutiny, and if not, what then do concepts like coordinate symmetries and invariances in the Theory of Special Relativity actual reveal to us about the nature of electricity and magnetism?
items.why_watch: This pushes back on the popular claim that electricity and magnetism are 'really the same thing' — a satisfying idea that turns out to rest on a shakier mathematical foundation than most explainers admit. Dialect is one of the few channels willing to challenge physics folklore rather than repeat it, and the argument here is careful and specific. Good viewing if you've ever felt slightly uneasy accepting that explanation.

For over half a century, the world’s greatest mathematicians — including Leibniz and the Bernoulli brothers — tried and failed to solve the Basel Problem, a question about the sum of the reciprocals of the square numbers. Along the w
items.why_watch: This covers the Basel problem — the search for a closed form of the infinite sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16... — which stumped mathematicians for decades until Euler cracked it with a genuinely surprising argument. At 38 minutes it's a commitment, but the payoff is a rare sense of watching a beautiful proof unfold at a pace that lets you actually follow the reasoning. The historical framing of who tried and failed makes the eventual solution land harder.

Why nothing can ever enter a black hole in the first place (not even light). We always talk about escaping from black hole, but from a certain perspective, nothing even enters a black hole. 

This video is sponsored by Ground News.
items.why_watch: The reframe here is genuinely interesting: instead of asking how anything could escape a black hole, the video asks whether anything actually enters one at all — a question that becomes meaningful when you think carefully about time dilation near the event horizon. FloatHeadPhysics uses spacetime diagrams rather than hand-waving, so the argument has real structure behind it. It's one of those videos that leaves you seeing a familiar concept from a completely different angle.

items.why_watch: A no-frills technical explainer on negative feedback in amplifiers, covering how it stabilizes gain, reduces distortion, and affects bandwidth. Production is basic, but the conceptual progression is clear and methodical — useful if you're studying electronics or need a refresher before working with op-amp circuits. Skip if you're looking for intuitive analogies; this one works through the math directly.

morning_soundtrack.title: Eric Slick Announces New Album Bounce House: Hear “Mannequin” (Feat. Molly Martin & Jamie Lidell)
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Eric Slick is the longtime drummer of the Philadelphia band Dr. Dog, and he's also got an extensive history of backing up other artists on record and onstage — Taylor Swift on her 2021 Maren Morris collab "You All Over Me," Waxahatchee and MJ Lenderman and Wilco's Sky Blue Sky fest earlier this year. Slick (what a cool name) also makes solo records, most recently 2024's New Age Rage . In March of 2027, Slick will return with Bounce House , his latest solo LP.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The kind of loose, collaborative energy that spills out of a late-night studio session into something unexpectedly joyful.

morning_soundtrack.title: XTC’s Colin Moulding Shares Second-Ever Solo Release Want It Bad (The Pep Talks And Playing Fields Of Old England)
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Colin Moulding is not the frontman of the UK psychedelic new wave cult heroes XTC; that's Andy Partridge. But Moulding has played bass, and sometimes sung lead and written songs, for the band since they first formed in 1972, and he's responsible for some of their best-known songs, including "Generals And Majors" and "Making Plans For Nigel." Moulding has also been in XTC side projects the Dukes Of Straosphear and TC&I. But Moulding does not make fully solo music very often. Today, he puts out the second solo release of his decades-long career.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Like finding a handwritten letter tucked inside a library book — rare, unhurried, and quietly thrilling.

morning_soundtrack.title: PUP, Wild Pink, Kevin Morby, & More Discuss Their Ratboys Covers For Singin’ To An Empty Chair Deluxe Edition Out Today
morning_soundtrack.snippet: Everyone loves Ratboys, including their esteemed indie rock peers. The tuneful, big-hearted Chicago quartet continued their streak of amazing albums with this year's Singin' To An Empty Chair , an album that backs some of Julia Steiner's most vulnerable lyrics yet with dynamic arrangements that suggest a band in full command of its powers.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The warm, communal glow of a house show where everyone in the room already knows all the words.

morning_soundtrack.snippet: You know the feeling of being wrapped up in high thread count sheets, so high they’re silky, and a perfect furry blanket that isn’t a cheap synthetic but just the right mix of soft and plush? I suppose asking that is like asking if you know
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Music that feels like being tucked in by someone who loves you, with nowhere to be until tomorrow.

morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: Sequined boots, a raised eyebrow, and a scandalous secret whispered across a honky-tonk barstool.

morning_soundtrack.title: Emma Ruth Rundle Releases a Brilliant Career-Defining Set
morning_soundtrack.snippet: This is the album Emma Ruth Rundle has long wanted and been destined to make. These Killing Times marks the actualization of a signature artist.
morning_soundtrack.vibe_check: The emotional equivalent of standing in the ruins of something beautiful and finally understanding why it had to fall.

global_silver_linings.title: Your Weekly Horoscope – ‘Free Will Astrology’ by Rob Brezsny
global_silver_linings.snippet: Our partner Rob Brezsny, whose latest book is Enlightenment for Rebels: Celebrating Our Wild and Sacred Earthly Selves, provides his weekly wisdom to enlighten our thinking and motivate our mood. Rob’s Free Will Astrology, is a syndicated weekly column appearing in over a hundred publications. He is also the author of Pronoia Is the Antidote for Paranoia: […]
global_silver_linings.reason: A weekly reminder that many people find comfort and reflection in pausing to consider the bigger picture of their lives — whatever lens they use to do that is worth celebrating. Taking time to look inward is a quietly radical act in a busy world.

global_silver_linings.title: A dying mother’s letter to her daughters about pain is a must-read for anyone facing uncertainty
global_silver_linings.snippet: "Walk through the fire and you will emerge on the other end, whole and stronger. I promise."
global_silver_linings.reason: In her final days, this mother chose to leave her daughters a gift of hard-won wisdom rather than silence — a testament to how love finds ways to reach forward through time. Her words remind us that honest, tender guidance can outlast any one life.

discovery_articles.title: Surviving the summer
discovery_articles.snippet: Editor in Chief Nancy Shute discusses existential threats to humankind: extreme heat, never-ending drought and a plan to provide Earth with sunlight on demand.
discovery_articles.ferns_note: Somewhere between the droughts and the heat domes, scientists are quietly drafting blueprints to act as the sun's dimmer switch — which is either the most audacious idea humanity has ever had, or a very good sign we've run out of smaller ones. The existential stakes here aren't hypothetical; they're already showing up in your summer forecast.

featured_read.title: College Sports Are Great
featured_read.snippet: The accomplishments of athletes are every bit as impressive and legitimate as those of dancers, debaters, and oboists.
featured_read.blurb: This essay makes a quietly radical case that the split-second precision of a point guard or a gymnast deserves the same cultural respect we extend to a violinist or a competitive debater. It asks why we've decided that only certain kinds of physical excellence count as serious.

reading_room.title: Emily Wilson Can’t Let The Odyssey Go
reading_room.snippet: The translator spoke about her desire to retranslate the epic—and her harsh review of the recent film.
reading_room.blurb: Emily Wilson, the scholar who gave us the first female English translation of The Odyssey, sits down to explain why she still can't leave it alone — and why the recent film adaptation made her wince in very specific, very illuminating ways.

reading_room.title: How Long Until AI Doesn’t Need Humans?
reading_room.snippet: She thinks it’s nearly imminent. He doesn’t.
reading_room.blurb: Two thoughtful people who disagree about when AI will render human labor optional talk it through in real time, and the gap between their timelines turns out to be more unsettling than either position alone. A conversation that earns its anxiety.

reading_room.title: This Dolphin Steals from Fish for Its Meals
reading_room.snippet: Putting a dent in dolphins’ reputation as the “good guys of the sea”
reading_room.blurb: It turns out dolphins have been quietly running a kleptoparasitism racket — stealing fish caught in human nets — and marine biologists are only now reckoning with what it reveals about animal cunning and our own need for oceanic heroes.

reading_room.title: Murder-in-Law
reading_room.snippet: "The twisted story of a domestic contract killing."
reading_room.blurb: A domestic contract killing unravels in ways that implicate not just a marriage but an entire architecture of secrets, loyalty, and mundane cruelty — the kind of true-crime story that lingers because the motive is almost ordinary.

reading_room.title: Lit Hub Weekly: September 14 – 18, 2026
reading_room.snippet: Don’t have time to read all those fall reading lists? That’s okay. We read them for you.
reading_room.blurb: Lit Hub distilled the season's avalanche of fall reading lists so you don't have to, and the result is less a roundup than a small argument about which books are actually earning their buzz right now.
